Buying guide / Pallet racking

Pallet racking types compared

The right pallet racking depends on how many SKUs you store, how many pallets you hold per SKU, how stock must rotate and what forklifts you use. Selective and wide-aisle racking give access to every pallet; very narrow-aisle (VNA) racking keeps that access while fitting about 40% to 45% more pallets; drive-in racking stores about 60% to 80% more pallets than selective but only gives access lane by lane; pallet flow racking enforces strict first-in, first-out rotation.

How to choose in five questions

  1. How many SKUs, and how many pallets per SKU? Many SKUs with few pallets each point to selective, wide-aisle or VNA racking. Few SKUs with many pallets each point to drive-in or pallet flow.
  2. Does stock have to rotate first-in, first-out? Expiry dates and batches favour pallet flow or drive-through racking. Drive-in racking works last-in, first-out.
  3. How expensive is floor space? When land or cold-store volume is costly, VNA (with access to every pallet) or drive-in (bulk) packs more pallets into the same building.
  4. What forklifts do you have or plan? Selective and wide-aisle racking work with standard counterbalance and reach trucks. VNA needs guided turret trucks and a very flat floor slab.
  5. How tall is the building? VNA layouts can use heights of 18 m and more; standard layouts are set by the reach of your forklifts.

Mixing systems in one warehouse

Most warehouses combine systems: selective or VNA racking for the full SKU range, drive-in or flow lanes for fast-moving bulk lines, and mezzanine floors or multi-tier shelving for small-item picking. ProRack engineers the whole layout together in Tekla Structures and RSTAB so the systems, aisles and handling equipment fit the building.

Questions

Frequently asked questions

Which pallet racking gives the most storage?

Drive-in racking stores about 60% to 80% more pallets than selective racking, but only the front pallet of each lane is accessible. If you need access to every pallet, very narrow-aisle (VNA) racking gives about 40% to 45% more pallets than a conventional wide-aisle layout.

What is the difference between selective and VNA racking?

Both give direct access to every pallet. Selective racking uses aisles of about 3.0 to 3.8 m for standard counterbalance and reach forklifts. VNA racking reduces aisles to about 1.5 m and uses guided turret trucks, which needs a very flat floor but stores more pallets on the same footprint.

Which racking is best for FIFO stock rotation?

Pallet flow racking gives strict first-in, first-out rotation because pallets loaded at the back roll forward to the picking face. Drive-through racking also works FIFO when loaded from one side and picked from the other.

Which racking suits cold storage?

Cold stores are expensive per cubic metre, so dense systems are common: drive-in racking for bulk pallets of few SKUs, or VNA racking when every pallet must stay accessible. The choice depends on the number of SKUs and how stock rotates.
